quests.question: If the recall had been issued a month earlier,
options: far fewer cars will be affected by the fault.
far fewer cars would have been affected by the fault.
far fewer cars would be affected by the fault.
far fewer cars are affected by the fault.
quests.correctAnswer: far fewer cars would have been affected by the fault.
quests.hint: A completed past decision with a completed past result — pure third conditional.
quests.explanation: Both the recall timing and the number of affected cars are finished past facts, so pure third conditional (past perfect + would have + past participle) is correct.

quests.question: If the recall hadn't been delayed by internal politics,
options: the company's reputation probably wouldn't have been in tatters right now.
the company's reputation probably won't be in tatters right now.
the company's reputation probably wouldn't be in tatters right now.
the company's reputation probably isn't in tatters right now.
quests.correctAnswer: the company's reputation probably wouldn't be in tatters right now.
quests.hint: A past delay shaping the company's present-day reputation.
quests.explanation: The delay was a past event, but the reputation damage is present ('right now'), so wouldn't + base verb ('wouldn't be') is correct.

quests.question: If regulators reviewed these reports more thoroughly,
options: issues like this would have surfaced much sooner in general.
issues like this surface much sooner in general.
issues like this will surface much sooner in general.
issues like this would surface much sooner in general.
quests.correctAnswer: issues like this would surface much sooner in general.
quests.hint: A general, ongoing hypothetical about regulatory practice.
quests.explanation: This is a general, ongoing hypothetical about how things could work, not one specific past event, so pure second conditional (past simple + would) is correct.

quests.question: Only if independent auditors confirm the figures,
options: the merger proceeds as planned.
the merger would proceed as planned.
the merger would have proceeded as planned.
the merger will proceed as planned.
quests.correctAnswer: the merger will proceed as planned.
quests.hint: 'Only if' stresses that this is the single required condition for the deal to proceed.
quests.explanation: 'Only if' emphasizes that independent audit confirmation is the one, single condition required for the merger to proceed; will + base verb expresses the real expected outcome once that condition is met. (In very formal writing, this could also be inverted: 'Only if... will the merger proceed' — but the standard order used here is equally correct.)

quests.question: Even if the figures check out perfectly,
options: some shareholders would have still voted against the deal on principle.
some shareholders still vote against the deal on principle.
some shareholders will still vote against the deal on principle.
some shareholders would still vote against the deal on principle.
quests.correctAnswer: some shareholders will still vote against the deal on principle.
quests.hint: 'Even if' shows some shareholders' vote doesn't depend on the numbers.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' signals that some shareholders' opposition isn't really dependent on the figures — their vote is presented as fixed regardless.

quests.question: In case the vote fails,
options: the board is already drafting an alternative proposal.
the board would already draft an alternative proposal.
the board already drafts an alternative proposal.
the board will already draft an alternative proposal.
quests.correctAnswer: the board is already drafting an alternative proposal.
quests.hint: 'In case' describes a precaution already being taken now.
quests.explanation: 'In case' motivates the board's current drafting work as a precaution, independent of whether the vote actually fails.

quests.question: If you're not into the movie,
options: we can just leave halfway through, no big deal.
we would have just left halfway through, no big deal.
we just leave halfway through, no big deal.
we will just leave halfway through, no big deal.
quests.correctAnswer: we can just leave halfway through, no big deal.
quests.hint: Casual, informal first-conditional phrasing, still following the core grammar rules.
quests.explanation: Even in casual speech, first conditional structure holds: a real present condition plus a real possible result, here expressed with 'can' for a relaxed, informal offer.

quests.question: Provided the necessary documentation is submitted in full,
options: the application is processed within the standard ten-day period.
the application would be processed within the standard ten-day period.
the application would have been processed within the standard ten-day period.
the application will be processed within the standard ten-day period.
quests.correctAnswer: the application will be processed within the standard ten-day period.
quests.hint: Formal, official register using 'provided'.
quests.explanation: 'Provided' suits this formal, official context, stressing the necessary condition; will + base verb gives the real expected outcome.

quests.question: Unless something wild happens,
options: I'll probably just stay in and relax tonight.
I probably just stay in and relax tonight.
I would have probably just stayed in and relaxed tonight.
I would probably just stay in and relax tonight.
quests.correctAnswer: I'll probably just stay in and relax tonight.
quests.hint: Casual, informal 'unless' phrasing about tonight's real plan.
quests.explanation: Even in relaxed, informal speech, 'unless' still means 'if...not' and pairs with a real, specific future plan, so will (contracted 'I'll') + base verb is correct.

quests.question: If the reviewer had read the manuscript in a different order,
options: her first impression of the plot twist is completely different.
her first impression of the plot twist might have been completely different.
her first impression of the plot twist will be completely different.
her first impression of the plot twist might be completely different.
quests.correctAnswer: her first impression of the plot twist might have been completely different.
quests.hint: A neutral, uncertain counterfactual about a completed past event.
quests.explanation: This refers to a specific, completed past reading experience, so third conditional (past perfect + might have been) is correct, with 'might' expressing genuine uncertainty.

quests.question: If the author hadn't reordered the chapters at the last minute,
options: critics will probably be praising a very different book right now.
critics would probably have been praising a very different book right now.
critics are probably praising a very different book right now.
critics would probably be praising a very different book right now.
quests.correctAnswer: critics would probably be praising a very different book right now.
quests.hint: A past editorial decision shaping the book's present-day reception.
quests.explanation: The reordering happened in the past ('at the last minute'), but critical reception is present ('right now'), so would + base verb ('would be praising') is correct.

quests.question: If endings like this were more common in the genre,
options: readers react less strongly to this particular twist.
readers might react less strongly to this particular twist.
readers will react less strongly to this particular twist.
readers would have reacted less strongly to this particular twist.
quests.correctAnswer: readers might react less strongly to this particular twist.
quests.hint: A general, ongoing hypothetical about genre conventions.
quests.explanation: This is a general hypothetical about the genre as a whole, not one specific past event, so pure second conditional (past simple + might) is correct.

quests.question: If the coach had rested her before the final,
options: she will perform even better in the last event.
she might have performed even better in the last event.
she performs even better in the last event.
she might perform even better in the last event.
quests.correctAnswer: she might have performed even better in the last event.
quests.hint: A neutral, uncertain counterfactual about a completed past event.
quests.explanation: This refers to one specific, completed past competition, so third conditional (past perfect + might have + past participle) is correct, with 'might' expressing genuine uncertainty.

quests.question: If she hadn't pushed through that early injury,
options: her career might already be over by now.
her career will already be over by now.
her career is already over by now.
her career might have already been over by now.
quests.correctAnswer: her career might already be over by now.
quests.hint: A past decision shaping her present-day career status.
quests.explanation: Pushing through the injury happened in the past, but her career status is present ('by now'), so 'might' + base verb ('might already be') fits the uncertain present result.

quests.question: If athletes had longer recovery windows between events,
options: injuries like hers could become far less common.
injuries like hers will become far less common.
injuries like hers become far less common.
injuries like hers could have become far less common.
quests.correctAnswer: injuries like hers could become far less common.
quests.hint: A general, ongoing hypothetical about sports policy.
quests.explanation: This is a general hypothetical about athletes in general, not one specific past event, so pure second conditional (past simple + could) is correct.

quests.question: If the renovation stays on budget,
options: we would have finally had the kitchen we've been planning for years.
we would finally have the kitchen we've been planning for years.
we'll finally have the kitchen we've been planning for years.
we finally have the kitchen we've been planning for years.
quests.correctAnswer: we'll finally have the kitchen we've been planning for years.
quests.hint: A real, specific plan depending on a real possible outcome.
quests.explanation: Staying on budget is a real, achievable possibility, so will (contracted 'we'll') + base verb expresses the genuine expected result.

quests.question: If the contractor could start any sooner,
options: we would probably move in before the holidays.
we probably move in before the holidays.
we will probably move in before the holidays.
we would have probably moved in before the holidays.
quests.correctAnswer: we would probably move in before the holidays.
quests.hint: The contractor's schedule is fixed — this imagines an unreal alternative.
quests.explanation: The contractor's start date isn't actually flexible, so this imagines a hypothetical alternative, using second conditional (past simple + would), despite the plausible-sounding real framing.

quests.question: If we hadn't gone over budget on the flooring,
options: we still have money left for the garden this year.
we will still have money left for the garden this year.
we would have still had money left for the garden this year.
we would still have money left for the garden this year.
quests.correctAnswer: we would still have money left for the garden this year.
quests.hint: A past spending decision affecting the present budget.
quests.explanation: Going over budget happened in the past, but having money left is a present state ('this year', ongoing), so would + base verb ('would still have') is correct.

quests.question: Only if you can show the original receipt,
options: you would have gotten a refund.
you get a refund.
you would get a refund.
you will get a refund.
quests.correctAnswer: you will get a refund.
quests.hint: 'Only if' stresses that this is the single required condition for a refund.
quests.explanation: 'Only if' emphasizes that showing the receipt is the single required condition; will + base verb expresses the real expected outcome once that condition is met.

quests.question: As long as the terms remain unchanged from here on,
options: both parties will continue to honor the original agreement.
both parties would continue to honor the original agreement.
both parties would have continued to honor the original agreement.
both parties continue to honor the original agreement.
quests.correctAnswer: both parties will continue to honor the original agreement.
quests.hint: 'As long as' expresses an ongoing condition for a real continued commitment.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' introduces an ongoing condition that must continue to hold; will + base verb expresses the real, expected continuation.

quests.question: Even if the numbers look better next quarter,
options: the board will likely stay cautious about further expansion.
the board would likely stay cautious about further expansion.
the board would have likely stayed cautious about further expansion.
the board likely stays cautious about further expansion.
quests.correctAnswer: the board will likely stay cautious about further expansion.
quests.hint: 'Even if' shows the board's caution doesn't really depend on next quarter's numbers.
quests.explanation: 'Even if' signals that the board's cautious stance is presented as fixed, not truly dependent on whether the numbers improve.

quests.question: Had the two departments shared data from the beginning,
options: this entire duplication of effort would have been avoided.
this entire duplication of effort would be avoided.
this entire duplication of effort will be avoided.
this entire duplication of effort is avoided.
quests.correctAnswer: this entire duplication of effort would have been avoided.
quests.hint: A formal inverted third conditional about a completed past situation.
quests.explanation: 'Had the two departments shared' inverts a completed past condition; would have been + past participle expresses the imagined past result.

quests.question: Were the two departments to finally share data going forward,
options: a lot of duplicated effort would disappear almost immediately.
a lot of duplicated effort will disappear almost immediately.
a lot of duplicated effort disappears almost immediately.
a lot of duplicated effort would have disappeared almost immediately.
quests.correctAnswer: a lot of duplicated effort would disappear almost immediately.
quests.hint: A formal inverted second conditional about a hypothetical future change.
quests.explanation: 'Were the two departments to share' inverts a hypothetical future possibility; would + base verb expresses the imagined consequence.

quests.question: Should the two departments ever formally merge,
options: reporting lines will need to be redrawn from top to bottom.
reporting lines need to be redrawn from top to bottom.
reporting lines would have needed to be redrawn from top to bottom.
reporting lines would need to be redrawn from top to bottom.
quests.correctAnswer: reporting lines will need to be redrawn from top to bottom.
quests.hint: A formal inverted first conditional about a real possible future event.
quests.explanation: 'Should the two departments ever merge' inverts a real, possible future event; will + base verb expresses the genuine expected consequence.

quests.question: If he weren't so instinctively private about money,
options: he will mention the inheritance to his siblings months ago.
he would have mentioned the inheritance to his siblings months ago.
he mentions the inheritance to his siblings months ago.
he would mention the inheritance to his siblings months ago.
quests.correctAnswer: he would have mentioned the inheritance to his siblings months ago.
quests.hint: An ongoing personality trait affecting one specific missed past action.
quests.explanation: Being private about money is an ongoing trait (present), but not mentioning the inheritance 'months ago' was a specific past event, so would have + past participle is correct.

quests.question: If the will had specified an equal split from the start,
options: the whole dispute between the siblings will never happen.
the whole dispute between the siblings never happens.
the whole dispute between the siblings would never have happened.
the whole dispute between the siblings would never happen.
quests.correctAnswer: the whole dispute between the siblings would never have happened.
quests.hint: A completed past cause with a completed past result — pure third conditional.
quests.explanation: Both the will's original wording and the resulting dispute are finished past facts, so pure third conditional (past perfect + would never have + past participle) is correct.

quests.question: If their grandmother hadn't written that letter years before she passed,
options: nobody will even know her original wishes today.
nobody would have even known her original wishes today.
nobody would even know her original wishes today.
nobody even knows her original wishes today.
quests.correctAnswer: nobody would even know her original wishes today.
quests.hint: A past action shaping present-day knowledge.
quests.explanation: Writing the letter happened years ago (past), but knowing her wishes is a present state ('today'), so would + base verb ('would even know') is correct.

quests.question: If the founders hadn't disagreed so bitterly over equity that first year,
options: the company would probably have still been a single, unified business today.
the company is probably still a single, unified business today.
the company would probably still be a single, unified business today.
the company will probably still be a single, unified business today.
quests.correctAnswer: the company would probably still be a single, unified business today.
quests.hint: A past falling-out shaping the company's entire present-day structure.
quests.explanation: The disagreement happened in a specific past year, but the company's current structure is present ('today'), so would + base verb ('would still be') is correct — the mixed conditional pattern at the heart of this whole curriculum.

quests.question: Were the two founders to reconcile now, after all these years,
options: it will still be far too late to undo the split.
it would still be far too late to undo the split.
it is still far too late to undo the split.
it would have still been far too late to undo the split.
quests.correctAnswer: it would still be far too late to undo the split.
quests.hint: A formal inverted second conditional imagining a present hypothetical reconciliation.
quests.explanation: 'Were the two founders to reconcile now' inverts a hypothetical present possibility; would + base verb expresses the imagined, still-unchanged consequence.

quests.question: Had the two of them handled that first disagreement differently,
options: the whole history of the company might unfold in a completely different way.
the whole history of the company might have unfolded in a completely different way.
the whole history of the company unfolds in a completely different way.
the whole history of the company will unfold in a completely different way.
quests.correctAnswer: the whole history of the company might have unfolded in a completely different way.
quests.hint: The final question of the curriculum: a formal inverted third conditional with genuine, reflective uncertainty.
quests.explanation: 'Had the two of them handled it differently' inverts a completed past condition; 'might have unfolded' expresses genuine, reflective uncertainty about an alternate past — full mastery of counterfactual reasoning.
